segments.text: Imagine you go for a routine health check, and the doctor suggests a quick screening test.
It looks for a condition that is fairly rare. About one in every hundred people your age has it.
The test is good. If you have the condition, it catches it nine times out of ten.
And if you are healthy, it only gives a false alarm one time in ten.
A few days later, the result comes back. Positive.
So, how worried should you be? What is the chance you actually have it?
Take a second, and make your own guess.
Most people say about ninety percent. After all, the test is ninety percent accurate.
Here's the surprise. The real answer is about eight percent.
Not ninety. Eight. Less than one in ten.
Nothing in that story is a trick. The test really is good. Your gut just left out one number.
How rare the condition was to begin with.
The tool that puts that number back in is called Bayes' theorem. And by the end of this video, you will be able to do this in your head.
Welcome to Math Lab TV. Where math is something you can see.
Today you will learn how to turn a test result into a real probability, just by counting people.
You will see Bayes' theorem as a formula, and exactly what every symbol means.
And you will see how evidence adds up, in spam filters, fraud alerts and machine learning.
This isn't just about medical tests.
Any time a rare thing meets an imperfect detector, the same trap is waiting.
A smoke alarm going off. An email flagged as spam. A message from your bank asking, was this you?
Each one is a positive test. And each one asks the same question: given this alarm, how likely is the real thing?
And smart people get this wrong. In one well known study, doctors were given a screening puzzle with numbers like ours.
Only about one in five picked the right answer. Almost half picked nine in ten.
That's not because doctors are bad at math. It's because the numbers came as percentages of percentages.
Change the form, and the problem becomes easy. So here is the trick for this whole video: stop thinking in percentages, and start counting people.
And Bayes isn't only about tests. It's a rule for changing your mind by the right amount when new evidence arrives. Not too little, and not too much.
Let's do it. Picture one thousand people, all taking the same test.
Each little square is one person. Forty across, twenty five down. One thousand.
Step one. How many of them have the condition? One in a hundred. So, ten people.
The other nine hundred and ninety are healthy.
Step two. Test the ten people who have the condition. It catches nine of them.
So, nine true positives, and one person the test misses.
Step three. Test the nine hundred and ninety healthy people. It wrongly flags one in ten of them.
That's ninety nine false alarms.
Now, look only at the people holding a positive result.
Nine of them actually have the condition. Ninety nine are healthy. One hundred and eight positives in total.
If your test is positive, you are one of these one hundred and eight. And only nine of them are sick.
Nine out of one hundred and eight. That's one in twelve, about eight percent.
The test did its job. It caught almost everyone who was sick.
But healthy people outnumber sick people ninety nine to one. So even a small false alarm rate creates a crowd of false alarms.
Here, the false alarms outnumber the real cases eleven to one.
And yes, the test really is ninety percent accurate overall. Nine true positives, plus eight hundred and ninety one healthy people correctly cleared. Nine hundred right answers out of a thousand.
And notice, the positive result still mattered. Before the test, your chance was one in a hundred. After it, one in twelve.
That's more than eight times higher. The test moved you a lot. It just didn't move you anywhere near certain.
And a negative result? Of the eight hundred and ninety two people who test negative, just one has the condition.
So a negative test drops your chance from one in a hundred to about one in nine hundred. That's very reassuring.
What we just did, counting people, is exactly Bayes' theorem. Let's write it the way you'll see it in books.
Here is the same crowd as a tree. One thousand people split into ten who have it, and nine hundred and ninety who don't.
Then each branch splits again by the test result. Nine and one on top. Ninety nine and eight hundred and ninety one below.
A positive result means you're on one of the two positive leaves. Nine, or ninety nine. That's all Bayes is doing.
First, the symbols. A capital P, with brackets, means the probability of whatever is inside.
A means having the condition. B means testing positive.
And this vertical bar means given. So, P of A given B is the chance you have the condition, given that you tested positive.
That's the number we want. And here is Bayes' theorem.
P of A given B equals P of B given A, times P of A, divided by P of B.
Now let's match each piece to our crowd.
P of A is the base rate. How common the condition is before any test. Ten in a thousand.
P of B given A is how good the test is at catching it. Nine out of ten.
Multiply those two, and you get the true positives. Nine in a thousand.
P of B, on the bottom, is the chance of testing positive at all. Real or false, that's one hundred and eight in a thousand.
Divide, and the thousands cancel. Nine out of one hundred and eight. The same answer we got by counting.
So the formula is just a short way of saying: real positives, divided by all positives.
The bottom part is where people slip. It hides the false alarms.
Written out in full, P of B is the true positives from the sick, plus the false alarms from the healthy.
Three names you'll hear. The base rate is called the prior. The answer is called the posterior. And P of B given A is called the likelihood.
Prior means before the evidence. Posterior means after.
So you tested positive, and your chance is now about one in twelve. What would a sensible doctor do next?
Test again. And here is the beautiful part. The answer from the first test becomes the starting point for the second.
Yesterday's posterior is today's prior.
Take our one hundred and eight positives. Nine are sick, ninety nine are healthy. They all take a second test.
To avoid fractions of people, picture ten times as many. Ninety people who have it, and nine hundred and ninety who don't.
The test catches nine in ten of the sick, and wrongly flags one in ten of the healthy. Same as before.
After a second positive: eighty one sick, and ninety nine healthy.
Eighty one out of one hundred and eighty. That's forty five percent.
One percent, then eight, then forty five. Each positive pushes the number up.
There's a neat shortcut here. Compare sick to healthy as odds.
Before any test, the odds are one sick person for every ninety nine healthy.
A sick person is nine times more likely to test positive than a healthy one. Ninety percent, versus ten.
So each positive multiplies the odds of having it by nine. One to ninety nine becomes nine to ninety nine, then eighty one to ninety nine.
A third positive makes it seven hundred and twenty nine to ninety nine. About eighty eight percent.
One important condition. This only works if the second test makes its mistakes independently of the first.
If you repeat the same test on the same sample, it might simply repeat the same false alarm. Then the second positive tells you much less.
That's one reason doctors often confirm with a different kind of test.
So what actually moves the answer? There are only three dials. The base rate, the hit rate, and the false alarm rate.
Let's turn the base rate dial first, and keep the test exactly the same.
At one in a hundred, we're at eight percent. At one in ten, it jumps to fifty percent.
Let's check that middle one by counting. With one in ten, a thousand people means one hundred sick, and the test catches ninety of them.
Nine hundred healthy, and one in ten flagged. Ninety false alarms. Ninety real, ninety false. Fifty percent.
And only when half the people have the condition does your gut's ninety percent finally become right.
The rarer the condition, the more the false alarms win.
Now turn the false alarm dial instead. Same base rate, one in a hundred, but a test that wrongly flags only one healthy person in a hundred.
Now there are about ten false alarms instead of ninety nine, and a positive means about forty eight percent.
And the hit rate dial? Push it from nine in ten all the way to perfect, and the answer barely moves. From about eight percent to about nine.
So, a rule of thumb. When the thing you're looking for is rare, the false alarm rate matters far more than the hit rate.
Now let's see where this shows up in the real world. The labels change, but the counting is the same.
Machine learning. A classifier is just a test run by a computer.
Engineers have names for our numbers. Catching nine out of ten sick people is called recall.
And nine out of one hundred and eight, the share of alarms that are real, is called precision.
When the thing you're looking for is rare, a model can have great recall and still terrible precision. That's the base rate at work.

That's why teams measure precision on data with the real base rate. On a balanced test set, half positive and half negative, our same test would show ninety percent precision. In the real world, about eight percent.
And here's a trap. A model that simply says healthy to everyone is ninety nine percent accurate, and completely useless.
Data science. Bayes is the engine of Bayesian statistics.
You start with a prior belief, say, about how often visitors to a website buy something, and update it as each day's data comes in.
Each day's posterior becomes the next day's prior. Exactly like our second test.
And before trusting any automated flag on a dashboard, a good analyst asks: of all the past flags, how many were real? That's precision again, measured on real data.
Finance. Banks run fraud detectors on card payments.
Fraud is rare, far rarer than one in a hundred payments. So even a detector as good as our test would flag mostly honest payments.
That's one reason many banks send a quick, was this you, message instead of simply blocking the card. In Bayes terms, your reply is a second, independent test.
The same idea applies to market signals. A warning sign that fired before most crashes may also fire in many calm years. Always ask how often it fires when nothing happens.
Computer science. Some of the first really effective spam filters were built on Bayes' theorem.
The prior is how much of all email is spam. The evidence is the words inside.
Each word nudges the odds up or down, just like each positive test. The filter multiplies them together.
To keep it simple, it treats every word as independent of the others. That shortcut is why it's called naive Bayes. It isn't true, but it works surprisingly well.
Computer security has the same problem. An intrusion alarm that fires on just one in a thousand normal logins can still bury the few real attacks under false alarms.
Before we wrap up, here are the three most common mistakes people make with Bayes.
Mistake one: flipping the question.
The chance of a positive test, if you're sick, is ninety percent. The chance you're sick, if you test positive, is about eight percent.
Same words, swapped around. Completely different numbers.
In courtrooms, this flip has a name: the prosecutor's fallacy. The chance of the evidence if someone is innocent is not the chance they're innocent, given the evidence.
Mistake two: ignoring the base rate.
Take the same test, but give it only to patients who already have symptoms. Say one in five of them has the condition.
Out of a thousand, that's one hundred and eighty true positives, against eighty false alarms. Now a positive means about seventy percent.
Same test. Same result. The base rate changed everything.
Mistake three: counting the same clue twice.
If two tests share the same weakness, or two news stories copy the same source, they are really one piece of evidence, not two.
Multiply them as if they were independent, and you'll end up far too confident.
And a bonus mistake: deciding the test is useless because the answer was only eight percent.
It isn't. A positive raised the chance more than eightfold, and a negative almost rules the condition out. A good test is a strong clue. It's just not a verdict.
Let's turn all of that into a recipe you can use for any yes or no question.
Step one: start with the base rate. How common is the thing, before any evidence?
Step two: picture a crowd. One thousand people usually avoids fractions.
Step three: split the crowd with the test. Count the true positives, and the false alarms.
Step four: keep only the people who match the evidence, and divide. Real cases, over all positives.
Step five: update. When new, independent evidence arrives, your answer becomes the new base rate.
For our test: one in a hundred to start. Nine real positives, ninety nine false alarms. About eight percent.
A test result is a clue, not a verdict. Bayes tells you how much the clue is worth.
Look around your world, and notice how many alarms are false alarms, and how rare the real thing usually is.
If this lesson made things clear for you, please subscribe to Math Lab TV, so we can keep building together.
But here's a puzzle for next time.
Scientists often report a number called a p-value, and it's very often described as the chance that a result is a fluke.
That description flips the question, just like mistake one.
Next time, we'll see what a p-value really measures, and why Bayes is the missing piece.
I will see you in the next video.
